title: 7 Ways Our Intuition Can Mislead Us About Learning
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler argues that teachers and students are routinely misled by their own impressions of what is working in the learning process, and that those impressions often contradict the scientific evidence. She walks through seven common beliefs, among them that phonics need not be systematic, that comprehension is a set of transferable skills, that students should act like experts, that instruction should match learning styles, that rereading is good study, that screens are as good as print, and that discovery beats explicit instruction. Her recurring move is to show why each belief feels true from inside the classroom, for example because early-grade decoding problems only surface years later, and then to set the research against it. She closes with a practical observation about change: shaming people for trusting their intuition backfires, so reform is more likely to come through better teacher preparation and appeals to shared goals.
points: Intuition about what works is unreliable because feedback is delayed, so elementary teachers rarely see the later reading failures their approach produces.
Expertise depends on stored factual knowledge, so asking novices to think like historians or scientists skips the foundation that makes analytical thinking possible.
Students misjudge their own learning, preferring rereading and screens because they feel easier even though retrieval practice and print produce better understanding.
Novices who watched an adult demonstrate a device succeeded, yet most claimed they could have worked it out alone, which shows how easily engagement is mistaken for learning.
Shaming practitioners for unscientific habits will not work; emphasising shared goals and better teacher-preparation content is the more promising route.
quotes: Evidence shows that many or even most kids do need this kind of instruction to become fluent “decoders” of written text—and fluent decoding is key to comprehension. But those who train reading teachers have generally resisted the evidence, and teachers’ intuition about what’s working can be misleading.

At one school I visited, a kindergarten teacher assured me her unsystematic approach to teaching reading was working beautifully. But fifth-grade teachers at the school told me they were shocked to discover many of their students couldn’t sound out simple words like pipe.

But experts can think the way they do only because they have enormous amounts of factual information about their fields stored in long-term memory. Education orthodoxy has frowned on getting kids to acquire factual information, dismissing it as “rote memorization,” but in fact it’s the necessary foundation for critical and analytical thinking.

People do have learning preferences, and there is evidence that it makes sense to convey information in more than one way—using both pictures and words, for example. But if a teacher or student believes that an “auditory learner” just can’t take in information through diagrams—when in fact that’s the most effective way to convey a particular concept—that will only make teaching and learning harder.

Researchers who conducted a series of studies on the effects of print and digital reading found that their subjects—college students—consistently believed they understood more when they read information on a screen. Just as consistently, the evidence showed they actually understood less.

There is in fact a large body of evidence showing that when learners are new to a topic, explicit instruction is far more effective than discovery or inquiry-based learning. But both teachers and students seem to have a bias in favor of the latter approaches, perhaps because they’re more engaging—and it’s easy to mistake engagement for learning.

One thing that’s unlikely to work is shaming people for engaging in practices that don’t line up with science. It’s a natural human tendency to trust our gut feelings—and it’s also natural to become defensive if people tell us we’re being foolish. A better bet is to emphasize shared goals, like ensuring that all teachers and students are as successful as possible.
